3.text: in magic, who consider themselves shamans. A female shaman in the Kolyma

4.text: country showed me a stone of a strange form, with two projections at one

5.text: end, similar to the two branches of a “wooden spirit.” It had a string tied

7.text: husband, and said she loved it much more than she did her living mate.

8.text: She assured me that most of her children were conceived from this stone.¹

9.text: Some personal “guardians” made of wood are carved with more care

10.text: than the usual crude wooden crotches. Some of these are represented in

11.text: Fig. 242. The second figure has a dog attached to it for hunting. We shall

12.text: find numerous figures of a similar character on the family charm-strings of

13.text: the Chukchee. Among carved animal faces we find the walrus, the polar

14.text: bear, the black bear, the wolf, and the raven. The dog is also a favorite,

15.text: because, as I have said before,² the dog or its image is supposed to give

17.text: When necessary, the figures can not only acquire life, but grow to very

18.text: large proportions. A woman who had two small figures of black bears told

19.text: me that ordinarily she kept them in her work-bag; but whenever she thought

20.text: she was in danger from spirits (for instance, if a contagious disease broke

21.text: out in the vicinity), she took the bears from the bag and put them on the

22.text: ground on either side of the entrance to the house. They were supposed to keep
